BOPEN.heard: Building virtual environments exam prep, key terms, camera, 20 ideas for aiming a game camera, from turning and moving it to changing its lens, telling a dolly from a zoom and following the player. With the exact word, an AI coding agent builds the shot you want.

BIDEA.heard: Hollow, this is Liam in for bear. Newcomers say zoom in when they mean move the camera closer. Those are two different things. A zoom changes the lens and the camera stays where it is. Adali moves the camera so near and far things shift against each other. This film goes through 20 camera terms in five groups, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.

BDEFS.heard: Four labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow. Glossary only, the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it. Computed, the numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs. Simulation, a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game. Conceptual, a drawing of the idea with no data behind it.

B0101.heard: This table is the map, 20 camera ideas in 5 groups and each one says what changed. The first group turns the camera on the spot with pan, tilt and roll. The direction changes and the position stays.

B0102.heard: The second group moves the camera. Dolly in and out truck pedestal in orbit. Here the position changes. A Dolly truck or pedestal keeps facing the same way, and an orbit turns to keep its subject in view.

B0103.heard: The third group changes the lens, zoom, focal length, field of view, and perspective versus orthographic. What changes is the angle the camera takes in and how big things look.

B0104.heard: The fourth group tells lookalikes apart with Dolly vs. Zoom and Parallax. The question here is whether near things and far things shift against each other.

B0105.heard: The fifth group follows the action. Follow camera, smoothing, also called damping, dead zone, look ahead, screen shake, and camera limits. These say how a camera trails a player waits, lades, jolts, and stops.

B0301.heard: Three small drawings of a camera that turns but never moves, the first is seen from above. Pan means turning left or right on the spot. Here the camera turns 25 degrees, its position unchanged and the red post comes into view. A pan turns while a truck moves sideways. For example, in a cutscene the camera stands by the gate and pans right from the player to a door that is just opened.

B0302.heard: The middle drawing is seen from the side. Tilt means turning up or down on the spot. The camera pitches up 25 degrees, its position unchanged, and the two upper posts turn red as they come into view. For example, at the start of a level the camera stands at the foot of a tower and tilts up to show the goal flag at the top.

B0303.heard: The last drawing shows what the camera sees. Role means spinning the camera around the direction it looks along so the horizon tips. Here it rolls 25 degrees and the flat ground now runs downhill across the picture. Pan and tilt change where the camera points and roll does not. For example, when the player's plane banks into a turn, the view rolls with it and the horizon slopes across the screen.

B0401.heard: A top view and a side view of a camera that moves but keeps facing the same way. Dolly means moving the camera forward or backward along the way it looks. Dolly in moves toward the subject and Dolly out moves away. Here the camera dolly's in 1.5 meters then back out. For example, before a boss fight the camera dolly's in toward the boss so it grows in the frame as the camera travels.

B0402.heard: Truck means moving the camera left or right while it keeps facing the same way. In the top view it trucks right and then left, 1.1 meters and the view cone never turns. A pan would turn the cone instead. For example, in a side-on cutscene the camera trucks right alongside a character running past a row of shops, looking straight at them the whole time.

B0403.heard: Pedestal means moving the camera straight up or down while it keeps facing the same way. In the side view it rises and falls 0.9 meters, still looking straight ahead. Tilt turns the camera upward and pedestal lifts the whole camera. For example, as the player rides an elevator up a shaft, the camera pedestals up with it, looking straight ahead the whole way.

B0501.heard: A top view of a subject in the middle of a circle. Orbit means moving around a subject on a curved path while keeping it framed. The camera sweeps 140 degrees around the circle, always 1.9 meters away and always aimed at the subject, so the subject never leaves the frame. For example, on a character select screen the camera orbits the chosen hero, so the player sees them from every side.

B0502.heard: Now a sweep done is a pan instead. The camera stays where it is and turns 70 degrees. Half its view is only 20 degrees wide so the subject passes out of the frame. An orbit keeps the subject and a pan can lose it. For example, if you ask an agent to circle the hero and it writes a pan, the hero drifts off the edge of the select screen.

B0701.heard: A top view of a camera fixed at the left. Zoom means changing the lens, its field of view, or focal length while the camera stays put. Here a 135mm lens narrows the cone to 15.2 degrees, and things look 3.86 times bigger than with a 35mm lens. A dolly would move the camera instead. For example, aiming down a scope in a first-person game zooms the view while the player stands still.

B0702.heard: Focal length is the strength of the lens in millimeters. A longer focal length gives a narrower view and more magnification. In the table with the sensor width, the drawing assumes 24 millimeters takes in 73.7 degrees and 200 millimeters only 10.3 at 5.71 times. For example, to make a far off castle fill the frame in a cutscene, give the camera a longer focal length rather than moving it.

B0703.heard: Field of view or FOV is the same lens described as an angle. A wider field of view shows more. At 90 degrees, seven of the nine posts are in view, and on the sensor assumed here that is an 18 millimeter lens. For example, a first-person game can offer a field of view setting in its options menu, and a wider setting shows more of the room at the edges of the screen.

B0801.heard: Two pictures of one scene, a dark house near the camera and a red tower far behind it. Dolly vs. Zoom comes down to parallax, near and far shifting against each other. In the Dolly the camera moves 1.2 meters forward. The near house grows 1.67 times and the far tower only 1.15. For example, a cutscene that Dolly's toward the hero makes the hero grow while the mountains behind barely change.

B0802.heard: Now the zoom the camera stays put in the lens magnifies 1.67 times. The house grows just as much as it did in the dolly, but now the tower grows 1.67 times 2. The zoom only magnifies. For example, zoom toward the same hero and the mountains behind swell along with them, and nothing shifts against anything else.

B0803.heard: Same house, different tower, compare the house's width to the towers. In the dolly, that ratio goes from 2.7 to 3.9. In the zoom, it stays at 2.7. That ratio is how you tell the two apart in a finished shot. For example, if the player grows much faster than the background, the camera moved, and if both grow together, it's zoomed.

B0901.heard: A top view of a camera beside three posts in a line and the picture it sees. Parallax means nearer things shift more than farther things when the viewpoint moves. The camera trucks one meter to the right. The posts were lined up and now they fan out in the picture. The zoom would scale everything by the same factor. For example, as a side-scrolling platformer follows the player, the near bushes rush past while the far hills creep.

B0902.heard: The bars give the shift for each post. The near post, two meters away, moves 110 pixels. The middle post at four meters moves 55, and the far post at eight meters moves 28, half the distance twice the shift. For example, a platformer with two background layers should move its far layer less than its near layer as the camera follows the player.

B1001.heard: Two rows of boxes that are all the same size in the world. Perspective means distant things shrink. Here the nearest box three meters away is 87 pixels wide, and the farthest at 30 meters is 20. The rows draw together toward the horizon. For example, a third person game use as a perspective camera, so an enemy far down a corridor looks small and grows as it comes nearer.

B1002.heard: Now the same box is seen by an orthographic camera. Orthographic mean size does not depend on distance. Every box is 44 pixels wide wherever it stands and the rows stay parallel and never meet. Perspective shrinks the far boxes and orthographic does not. For example, a puzzle game seen from above at an angle can use an orthographic camera, so a crate at the back of the room is drawn the same size as one at the front.

B1201.heard: A view window over a moving red dot in this simulated run. A follow camera tracks a moving target, usually with smoothing. In the top lane, the window is locked to the target. The camera's position equals the targets on every frame, so the lag is zero pixels. For example, in a platformer, the camera follows the player across the level, so the player stays on screen while they run.

B1202.heard: Smoothing also called damping spreads the camera's catch up over time, so it trails the target slightly instead of snapping to it. In the lower lane the window falls behind as the dot speeds up by as much as 103 pixels then eases in and settles at zero. The time constant is 0.25 seconds. For example, when the player dashes a smoothed camera lags a moment and glides after them instead of jerking.

B1301.heard: A screen frame with a dashed box in the middle in this simulated run. A dead zone is a region of the screen where the target can move without the camera moving. The red dot walks right inside the box and the view stays still. At the edge of the box, 70 pixels from the center the camera follows, and all it moved 270 pixels. For example, a platformer hero can shuffle back and forth without the screen jiggling.

B1302.heard: Look ahead shifts the framing toward the direction of travel. The target moves right at 200 pixels per second, and the frame looks half a second ahead to where the target will be so it shifts 100 pixels forward. The dot sits behind the center cross with room in front, a dead zone waits and look ahead leans. For example, in a runner game the camera shows more ground ahead of the running player so they see the next gap in time to jump.

B1401.heard: A small view of a scene in this simulated run. Screen shake is a brief fading random offset of the camera for impact. A hit lands and the view jumps by up to 80 pixels in a random direction, less on every frame until the most it can jump is 0.6 pixels. Shake ads jerk on purpose and smoothing takes it away. For example, when an enemy's attack hits the player, the screen jolts for a moment, so the hit is felt.

B1402.heard: The graph traces the sideways offset over 0.6 seconds. The black line jumps from side to side but stays inside the red dashed curve which keeps falling. It drops to 5% 0.9 pixels after 0.54 seconds and the shot is steady again. For example an explosion behind the player can shake the view hard at first and then let it settle fast so play goes on.

B1501.heard: A long strip of level with a hatched empty area past its right edge in this simulated run. Camera limits are clamps that keep the view inside the level. Without them the view follows the target to 590 and its right edge ends up 70 pixels past the end of the level. The player sees the void. For example, when the hero reaches the last wall of a level, a camera without limits shows empty space beyond it.

B1502.heard: Now with camera limits, the view center is clamped between 120 and 520 so its edges never leave the level. The target still walks on to 590 and the view stops at the edge. A dead zone is a box on the screen and limits are the edges of the level. For example, give the platformer camera limit so it stops at the left wall of the first room.

B1601.heard: Each pair puts two look-alike moves side by side. Pan turns the camera on the spot, here 40 degrees, and it stays in the same place. Truck moves the camera sideways, here's 0.7 meters, still facing the same way.

B1602.heard: Dolly moves the camera forward here 1.2 meters and its view angle stays at 46 degrees. Zoom keeps the camera put and narrows the angle to 22 degrees. Both make the subject bigger in different ways.

B1603.heard: Orbit moves the camera around the subject on a curve and the subject stays framed. Pan turns the camera on the spot and here the subject is lost from view.

B1604.heard: Smoothing or damping starts moving at once and eases toward the target, trailing slightly. The red line is the target and the black line the camera. A dead zone camera waits then follows and stops short of the target.

B1701.heard: Vague requests on the left, each with the exact instruction that replaces it. Swoop-in becomes dolly in 2 meters, 1.5 seconds, ease out. The graph shows it start at 4 meters per second and slow to zero as it arrives.

B1702.heard: Look around a bit becomes pan-right 40 degrees, 2 seconds, easing out. That means slow, fast, slow, with a top speed of 59 degrees per second.

B1703.heard: Get closer could mean a dolly or a zoom and the exact version picks one. Zoom from 35mm to 85mm in one second, easing out and the camera stays put. The angle narrows from 54.4 degrees to 23.9.

B1704.heard: Make the hit feel heavier becomes screen shake 0.3 seconds 12 pixels fading to zero. The curve shows the shake shrinking with 5% left at 0.3 seconds.

B1705.heard: Follow the player nicely becomes, follow with smoothing, a 0.25 second time constant, and a dead zone 140 by 100 pixels. The camera closes 95% of the gap after 0.75 seconds, three time constants.

B1801.heard: This is a checklist to run before you give a camera instruction. First is the camera moving with a dolly, truck, pedestal or orbit or turning with a pan, tilt or roll.

B1802.heard: Second is it the legs or the lens. A dolly moves the camera and a zoom changes the lens. Only the dolly makes near and far things shift against each other.

B1803.heard: Third, did you name the axis, the direction, how far or how many degrees, how long and the easing, and AI coding agent cannot guess any of them.

B1804.heard: Fourth, for a camera that follows a player, give the smoothing amount, the dead zone size, the look ahead, and the camera limits.

B1805.heard: Fifth for a hit give the shake size and how long it lasts and say that it fades to zero.

B1806.heard: Sixth, for the lens and projection, give the focal length or the field of view and say perspective or orthographic. Then say it exactly. Dolly in 2 meters, 1.5 seconds, ease out, not swoop in.

BVDT.heard: Let's recap, pan, tilt, and roll turn the camera on the spot. Dolly, truck, and pedestal move the camera and keep it facing the same way. An orbit circles the subject and keeps it framed where a pan can lose it. A zoom changes the lens and a Dolly moves the camera. Parallax means near things shift more than far ones when the camera moves. A dead zone waits, smoothing trails, look ahead leads, and limits stop the view.

BHTF.heard: Quizmy on camera terms with short game-making cases one at a time. Use pan tilt, truck, pedestal, dolly, zoom, orbit, parallax, dead zone and look ahead. Describe what a camera does in a game or a cutscene and I must name the exact term and say why its look alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply then tell me if I was right.

BOUT.heard: Key terms camera at Nick Bear Brown.
